items.title: Trump closes an AI loophole
items.summary:
President Donald Trump departs the White House on November 16, 2026, ahead of a trip to China and the Philippines. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images 

This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is closing a global AI chip loophole that the Jensen Huang scandal put in the spotlight.

What’s changing? The Commerce Department is trying to make it harder for China to access top-of-the-line AI microchips like those made by Nvidia.

Currently, China is able to dodge export rules by renting computing power from third-country data centers, which can legally buy American-made chips that China can’t.

But under the rule issued Monday, which is set to take effect in 90 days, data centers in a handful of countries will face new export restrictions on chips — including a requirement that they perform “robust due diligence on their customers” to make sure that they aren’t evading an export ban. 

What’s the context? Huang, who resigned from Nvidia last week, was brought down in part by his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an alleged Chinese spy ( kind of ) and an executive at a Singapore-based tech company, Megaspeed, that was renting compute to Chinese firms — exactly the kind of thing that the new rule aims to crack down on. 

What’s the big picture? The Nvidia scandal is front and center. But under the hood, there’s also some Trump administration infighting going on. As a statement…
items.t: Trump closes an AI loophole

items.title: How to actually fix America’s air traffic control system
items.summary:
What happened on Friday was only the latest symptom of an aging air traffic control system. | Adam Gray/Getty Images 

On Friday evening, in the midst of the second-longest closure ever of US airspace, I bought two plane tickets and found myself contemplating, possibly for the first time, the list of hidden fees tacked onto my fare. 

I had forked over $16.95 for a US transportation tax, plus $5.30 for a flight segment tax, both of which pool into the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, which will ultimately contribute to the Federal Aviation Administration’s work, thereby ensuring that my flight from New York to Florida lands smoothly. 

But though one might expect my $22.25 — enough to pay an air traffic trainee’s salary for about an hour — would go directly into the FAA’s coffers, it does not. In fact, the FAA needs to get congressional approval every time it taps into its trust fund, a political bottleneck that has for decades kept the FAA from making the critical long-term modernization projects it needs to make sure that a single botched cable job is not enough to bring down the busiest airspace in the world.

In the days since all air travel shut down across the United States, we’ve learned a great deal about what happened and why. But the best response to the crisis — and the path to preventing it from happening again (and again and again) — may well be found in shortening the path that my $22.25 takes on its way to the beleaguered agency that needs it so badly. It’s a solution that transformed air travel in Canada — which turned its air traffic control system around…
items.t: How to actually fix America’s air traffic control system

items.title: What the midterms taught us
items.summary:
Newly elected members of Congress pose for a group photograph on the steps of the US Capitol Building on November 12, 2026, in Washington, DC | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 

Everyone from party insiders to the pundits have now parsed the results from the midterm elections, and few races are left to call. Soon, the political world will turn its sights to the 2028 presidential election — but first, America, Actually is taking a moment to reflect on eight months of reporting across the country. 

That included anger about the construction of a data center in southern New Jersey ; Democratic hopes for a governing trifecta in Wisconsin , understanding the “Trump slump” — a combination of the pain from tariffs and the fear of immigration enforcement — in Las Vegas ; and hearing voters in a crucial swing district in Pennsylvania connect the war in Iran with high gas prices. 

No one votes for president in 2027, but the issues that we saw on the road are a reminder that politics doesn’t only live in the voting booth (and, of course, they’ll have implications for 2028).

This week on America, Actually, I spoke with host Astead Herndon about the moments that we just can’t stop thinking about from our reporting.

Below is an excerpt from that conversation, focusing on two aspects of this year’s midterms: how the results could reverberate in the GOP presidential race and what Angie Nixon’s close loss in her Senate race in Florida says about who the Democratic Party establishment will choose to support as the 2028 presidential primary gets underway in 2027. It has been edited for length…

items.title: Donald Trump loves Jensen Huang. Everyone else…
items.summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Nvidia/Japan AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo on July 16, 2026. | Philip Fong/AFP via Getty Images 

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company.

But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world. And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution.

Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies. That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution.

His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful. Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president.

This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum. It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment , who want to win an AI race against China. It includes economic populists in both parties,…
items.t: Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall

items.title: Being single can be a gift. Here’s how to embrace it.
items.summary:
When you’re single, it’s hard to avoid questions about your dating life. “Are you seeing anyone?” people will ask. “Had any fun dates?” 

Well-meant as it may be, these questions can leave you feeling less than, like you’ve failed in something that you were supposed to have figured out by now. At their worst, frequent questions about your love life imply that you don’t have love at all. 

Because we all learn, sooner or later, that there’s an expected direction of travel in life: Get an education; then a job. Fall in love and get married. Buy a house. Have children. And, of course, if you tick all those boxes, the expectation is that you’ll live happily ever after. 

Our rational brains understand this is just a fairy tale. But the gravitational pull of its mythic expectations can feel impossible to withstand — hence those questions as you catch up with friends at happy hour or pass the cranberry sauce during the holidays. And it isn’t just social pressure; there are numerous policies and tax breaks that incentivize marriage and children . The architecture of our society is built for couples, so if you’re single — whether by choice or by circumstance — how should you live? 

Who better to ask than a nun? 

Anne Curtis is a Sister of Mercy and the executive director of Mercy by the Sea , a retreat center in Madison, Connecticut. As a young woman, she made a vow to dedicate her life to God, which meant remaining single; it didn’t mean withdrawing from love — but allowing for more of it. 

If you’re imagining a stern old lady dressed in a habit, let me quickly disabuse you of…
items.t: Being single can be a gift. Here’s how to embrace it.

items.title: Democrats could raise the minimum wage next year. How high should they go?
items.summary:
A decade after the Democratic Party rallied around the Fight for 15 movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economic question for the new majority. | Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images 

In the wake of the midterm elections in which Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate , a growing number of politicians and activists have begun calling, publicly and privately, for Congress to seize the moment and pass the first federal minimum wage increase in 17 years. 

After running campaigns centered on the cost of living, Democrats and their allies say raising the $7.25 federal minimum closer to a “living wage” — i.e., enough for a full-time worker to cover basics like rent, food, and healthcare — is the obvious next step for their affordability mandate. A minimum wage increase also has a political advantage because businesses, not the government, cover the cost, meaning it has little effect on the deficit and doesn’t compete with other priorities for federal dollars.

“I’ve been talking with a lot of different Democrats on the Hill and they’ve been calling it a first 100-day issue,” said Jared Bernstein, who chaired President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers and is now at the liberal Center for American Progress. 

Rahm Emanuel, who is widely expected to run for president in 2028, has been urging Democrats to act , and it was a top issue for the party when he ran its campaign arm in 2006. “Pass a minimum wage $20 by 2030,” he said on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast after the election. Sen. Bernie Sanders…

items.title: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
items.summary:
On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.

The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.

Regional flavour

Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.

By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.

items.title: Men weren’t always “bad at friendship”
items.summary:
Summer's Eve (1893) by Norwegian painter Halfdan Egedius. | Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images 

The headlines may be dominated by artificial intelligence and electoral politics, but beneath it all, another debate constantly simmers, forever threatening to erupt.

I write, of course, of the great male friendship debate.

On one side: writers, journalists, and academics who fret over rising male loneliness , the emotional impact of friendless men on their partners , and the threat to society posed by atomized and isolated fellas. On the other: those who defend male friendships built around shared activities rather than heart-to-hearts.

These arguments often talk past each other. But the historian Tiffany Watt Smith offered me a way to think differently about both: that the gender roles undergirding the conversation are not nearly as fixed as they seem.

“I can definitely tell you that men in the past had much more intimate and romantic and involved friendships than we see today, for sure,” said Smith, who has published a number of books on the histories of friendship and emotions . “The idea that women are the kind of great experts in friendship is a really modern idea.”

I talked with Smith about Aristotle’s idea of the “perfect” friendship (it has to be between two dudes), how gendered notions of friendship inverted in the 19th century, and what men seeking deeper emotional connection from their buddies can learn from the past. You can hear that conversation and and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.

items.t: Men weren’t always “bad at friendship”

items.title: Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?
items.summary:
An angler displays a lake trout, considered an invasive species, that they caught on Lake McDonald in Glacier National Park in Montana on October 18, 2023. | Josh Edelson/AFP via Getty Images 

On a summer day in 1992, a man dumped a cooler full of a fish called yellow perch into Lake Mary Ronan, in northwest Montana. 

We know this because two teenagers saw him do it; they wrote down his license plate number and called in a tip to the Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks department (FWP), which immediately dispatched biologists to capture and kill the perch with nets and poison. 

The teenagers got a reward of $500 each for their efforts, while the man was charged with illegally introducing non-native fish into the lake, slapped with a small fine, and sent on his way. The law changed soon after: Now, intentionally introducing a non-native, invasive species to Montana’s waters is a felony punishable by as long as two years in prison or a fine of up to $25,000, or both. 

Why I wrote about this 

I visited Flathead Lake Biological Station in October, and while I was there I heard from a biologist about this strange, totally avoidable, invisible catastrophe in the making. I was absolutely fascinated — as I looked at the lake, I hardly believed it could lose its signature clarity because of a bucketful of fish — and decided I had no choice but to open this can of worms.

But the perch? The yellow perch — at least two of them — survived, multiplied, and quickly went on to wreak havoc. They established dominance in the lake, wiping out its population of a native fish called the…
items.t: Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?

items.title: Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
items.summary:
The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images 

In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate.

Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions. Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process. But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025.

It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment. Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way. There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education.

Yes, you read that right: sex ed. But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which…
items.t: Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten

items.title: “A rich message, but a poor campaign”: How Scott Colom beat the odds in Mississippi
items.summary:
Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS) speaks during a victory celebration for Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi, on November 11, 2026. | Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images 

On Wednesday, Mississippi’s Senate race was officially called for Democrat Scott Colom, who will become the first Black person to represent the state in the US Senate since Reconstruction, more than 140 years ago. Colom’s win is a stunning, historic upset — and for many Black Democrats, like Rep. Bennie Thompson, it’s been a long time coming.

Thompson, who also won his race last week, has represented Mississippi’s majority-Black Second Congressional District since 1993. Over the years, the 78-year-old lawmaker has frequently invoked the story of his father, who was never able to cast a vote because of racist Jim Crow laws that enforced segregation until the mid-1960s.

I sat down with Thompson for Today, Explained to talk about Colom’s run for Senate, how he won, what it means for Thompson personally. 

Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

Your dad was never able to cast a vote during his lifetime because of Jim Crow laws. And I wonder, growing up in Mississippi, what did you learn about who was allowed to participate in democracy?

items.title: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints | Letters
items.summary:
An investigator writes that a human-written grievance at least gets to the heart of the issue immediately. Plus letters from Dexter Jandoo and Pete Bibby

Re your article (‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints.

You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complaints process is accessible to tenants, but AI-generated complaints don’t help with this. Sending a complaint can be intimidating and time-consuming, and using AI can give someone confidence, but when we speak to customers in person or over the phone, and reference the same technical language that’s in their AI-generated complaint letter, they often don’t understand what we are saying.

items.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
items.summary:
When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so…
items.t: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence

items.title: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study
items.summary:
Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles.

In a new study, my colleagues and I used satellite tags to track young green turtles in a protected wetland in Sharjah, UAE. Our results reveal just how important these remaining natural spaces are to young turtles.

But we also found that nature can find a way to thrive in unexpected, human-made environments too. So protecting these habitats and the connections between wetlands, artificial environments and the open sea is essential to ensuring wildlife can persist in an increasingly human-shaped world.

Coastal wetlands protect our shorelines from storms, store carbon and provide important nursery habitats for marine life. Yet scientists still know surprisingly little about how marine wildlife, including turtles, sharks and rays, use these environments. Knowing where these animals feed, shelter and move helps identify which areas need protection and whether existing protected areas are working.

Our study, a collaborative effort between the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), a UAE government agency, the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre, focused on Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah, a marine protected area encompassing the last major coastal wetland ecosystem on the UAE’s east coast, which is called Khor Kalba.

Its complex wetlands support migratory wading…
items.t: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study

items.title: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong
items.summary:
Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill.

According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X, the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”.

In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems.

This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters.
items.t: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong

items.title: Sadiq Khan joins Labour figures urging PM not to water down electric vehicle targets – as it happened
items.summary:

On the Today programme this morning, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, a prominent leftwinger, indicated she might vote against legislation to implement the Alan Milburn proposals. She said she was concerned by the idea that the cuts would apply to people already getting sickness and disability benefits, and she said it appeared to be a breach of a promise given last year that people already getting Pip (the personal independence payment) would not lose it.

She said:

I just don’t think that you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work.

The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already in work. So I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second.

Milburn said he concluded fundamental change was needed. He said:

The whole system needs to be changed, because the system is geared to keeping people inactive when, for young people in particular, it’s all about how can you make them active, get them earning, learning, so that they can rely on a wage rather than on a benefit. So, this is not about cutting one benefit, it’s about rebuilding the system from scratch.

He said that he decided existing claimants should be covered by the changes, not just new changes.

It’s a big rewriting of the welfare system. And obviously one of the conundrums was, ‘Should this apply to only new claimants?’

I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not…

items.title: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef
items.summary:
As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species.

This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home.

The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken.

As the years went by, commercial jetliners superseded transatlantic sea travel, and the vessel was retired and neglected for decades. Rather than facing the ignominy of a breaker’s yard, the legendary ship was bought by Okaloosa County, Florida, to turn it into a diving attraction.

The SS United States is a particularly enormous structure to introduce to the seabed – longer even than the Titanic. It will rest in around 55 metres of water,…
items.t: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef

items.title: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis
items.summary:
What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit?

Across Europe, parts of the nationalist right are increasingly blurring the distinction between culture and ethnicity. The result is a view of national identity where belonging depends on where a person’s ancestors come from.

This way of thinking is called ethnonationalism – where membership of a nation depends on ethnic background or ancestry, rather than simply on citizenship or cultural identity.

In Denmark, where I live, this idea has recently taken a striking turn. A few months ago, I appeared in a televised debate opposite a former political adviser to a Danish right-wing party who, in essence and quite seriously, argued that to be Danish, you have to be able to tolerate milk.

The argument draws on the fact that the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, is more common among people with Northern European ancestry. The suggestion was that this biological trait…
items.t: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis

items.title: Ukraine peace talks end with no breakthrough – but Europe may be set to return from the cold
items.summary:
The first talks between Russia and Ukraine in nine months have concluded. The most positive thing that can be said about the US-mediated meeting in Abu Dhabi was that the dialogue did not break down and the parties seemed to agree to further meetings.

There was also at least one tangible result. Russia and Ukraine agreed on a large-scale exchange of prisoners of war, the magnitude of which will be clarified over the coming days. Beyond this, however, there were few signs of progress towards a peace agreement.

Despite Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky’s claim that all participants in the negotiation process “genuinely want to achieve a result before 2027”, the most important issues remain unresolved. These include ceasefire terms, the future status of occupied regions and long-term security guarantees for Ukraine.

The talks took place against the backdrop of continued fighting on the frontline. Russia’s military currently controls about a fifth of Ukraine, but progress on the battlefield has slowed in 2026 – and has even been reversed – due to Ukrainian…
items.t: Ukraine peace talks end with no breakthrough – but Europe may be set to return from the cold

items.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
items.summary:
Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others?

How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation.

The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly than the other varieties. This theory, I should point out, is based on my lived experience rather than any clinical expertise or any kind of research. Sorry – I felt too ill to bother with anything of the kind.

items.t: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
